items.prompt: What is the glow of certain fungi in a wood at night called?

options.label: Foxfire
options.feedback: An old name for rotting wood that shines.

options.label: Marshlight
options.feedback: That is burning gas over a swamp, not a fungus.

options.label: Firedamp
options.feedback: That is an explosive gas in coal mines.

options.label: Corpse candle
options.feedback: A folklore term for a different apparition.

items.ok_line: Foxfire — a name older than any explanation of it.
items.ko_line: The word has nothing to do with foxes, and everything to do with rotting wood.
items.exp_title: A name older than the science
items.exp_text: Foxfire is the pale green glow given off by decaying wood colonised by certain fungi. It has been noticed for as long as people have walked in woods at night: Aristotle wrote about cold light from wood, and Pliny described glowing stumps. The name probably comes from the Old French for false rather than from the animal — a false fire, giving light without heat.

items.prompt: What part of a glowing fungus produces the light?

options.label: The threads growing through the wood
options.feedback: Often the mycelium rather than the mushroom.

options.label: Only the cap of the mushroom
options.feedback: In many species the cap does not glow at all.

options.label: The spores as they are released
options.feedback: Spores are far too small and too few.

options.label: The bark it is growing on
options.feedback: Wood alone never glows.

items.ok_line: The glow is usually in the network, not the mushroom.
items.ko_line: The mushroom is only the fruit. The fungus itself is the part inside the wood.
items.exp_text: A mushroom is only the fruiting body; the fungus itself is a network of fine threads called mycelium, spread through the wood or soil. In many glowing species it is that hidden network that shines, which is why a piece of rotten log glows all over and no mushroom is in sight. Some species glow in the cap instead, and a few in both.

items.prompt: Roughly how many species of fungi are known to glow?

options.label: Around a hundred
options.feedback: Out of many tens of thousands described.

options.label: Around ten
options.feedback: Rather more than that have been found.

options.label: Around ten thousand
options.feedback: Glowing remains rare among fungi.

options.label: Nearly all of them
options.feedback: The vast majority give off no light at all.

items.ok_line: About a hundred, and new ones are still being described.
items.ko_line: It is a small club — a hundredth of a per cent of known fungi, near enough.
items.exp_text: Around a hundred glowing species are known, out of well over a hundred thousand described fungi. Almost all belong to a few related groups, which suggests the ability arose once and was kept, rather than being invented repeatedly. New ones are still turning up, several of them found only in the last twenty years — partly because you have to be in the right forest, at night, with your torch off.

items.prompt: Which mushroom is famous for its bright green glow?

options.label: The jack-o'-lantern
options.feedback: Its gills glow, and it is often mistaken for a chanterelle.

options.label: The field mushroom
options.feedback: The common edible mushroom does not glow.

options.label: The fly agaric
options.feedback: Red with white spots, and entirely dark at night.

options.label: The truffle
options.feedback: It grows underground and gives off no light.

items.ok_line: And it is poisonous, which makes the confusion worse.
items.ko_line: It is orange, it grows in clumps on wood, and people mistake it for a good edible.
items.exp_text: The jack-o'-lantern is a bright orange mushroom that grows in clumps at the base of trees, and its gills give off a green glow strong enough to see once your eyes adjust. It is regularly confused with the chanterelle and it is poisonous — severely upsetting rather than deadly. One reliable difference is that it grows on wood, while chanterelles grow from soil.

items.prompt: What colour is the light of glowing fungi?

options.label: Green
options.feedback: A pale yellow-green, in every known species.

options.label: Blue
options.feedback: Blue belongs to the sea, not to fungi.

options.label: Red
options.feedback: No fungus is known to glow red.

options.label: It varies by species
options.feedback: The brightness varies; the colour barely does.

items.ok_line: Green, every time, wherever in the world you find them.
items.ko_line: Unlike the sea, fungi have settled on a single colour worldwide.
items.exp_text: Every glowing fungus known shines in the same narrow band of yellow-green, around 520 nanometres — the part of the spectrum a dark-adapted human eye is most sensitive to. Brightness varies enormously, from a glow you need twenty minutes of darkness to notice up to a light said to be readable by. But the colour does not change, which is further evidence the ability has a single origin.

items.prompt: What is the leading explanation for why fungi glow?

options.label: It attracts insects that spread the spores
options.feedback: Insects come to the light and carry spores away.

options.label: It frightens animals that would eat it
options.feedback: A soft green glow frightens very little.

options.label: It helps the fungus find its food
options.feedback: A fungus does not hunt or search.

options.label: It warms the wood it grows in
options.feedback: The light gives off essentially no heat.

items.ok_line: A lamp put out to hire a courier.
items.ko_line: A fungus that cannot move has one big problem: getting its spores somewhere else.
items.exp_text: A fungus cannot move, so it must persuade something else to carry its spores. Experiments with sticky artificial mushrooms — some lit, some not — found far more insects arriving at the glowing ones. Several species also glow on a daily rhythm, brightening at night when the insects fly and dimming by day, which is hard to explain unless the light is meant to be seen.

items.prompt: Why does glowing wood give off no heat?

options.label: Almost all the energy becomes light
options.feedback: A chemical reaction, not a fire.

options.label: The wood is too damp to warm up
options.feedback: Dampness is not what keeps it cool.

options.label: The heat escapes into the ground
options.feedback: There is essentially no heat to escape.

options.label: It glows too faintly to warm anything
options.feedback: Even a bright example stays cold.

items.ok_line: Cold light, and that is what made it seem magical.
items.ko_line: Nothing is burning. So where would heat come from?
items.exp_text: Biological light comes from a chemical reaction that turns nearly all its energy into photons rather than heat, so a glowing log is exactly as cool as the wood beside it. That is what made foxfire so strange to earlier observers: fire meant heat, and here was light that could be carried in a pocket. Miners are said to have used pieces of it underground, where a flame would have been lethal.

items.prompt: What does a glowing fungus feed on?

options.label: Dead and rotting wood
options.feedback: It breaks down what no animal can digest.

options.label: Living leaves on the tree
options.feedback: These species work on wood already dead.

options.label: Insects it traps in the dark
options.feedback: Fungi do not trap insects for food.

options.label: Minerals dissolved in rain
options.feedback: Minerals alone carry no energy.

items.ok_line: It eats the wood, and the glow is a by-product of doing so.
items.ko_line: Foxfire appears on rotting logs. That is a clue about the diet.
items.exp_text: Glowing fungi are mostly wood-rotters, breaking down the lignin that makes timber rigid — something almost nothing else on Earth can digest. Without them, dead trees would pile up unrotted. The light appears to be tied to that chemistry, one step of the process producing the reactive molecule the glow needs. Useful work, with the light as a side effect that was later put to use.

items.prompt: How is it possible to make a plant glow using fungal genes?

options.label: The fungal chemistry runs on a plant molecule
options.feedback: Plants already make the raw material.

options.label: The fungus is grown inside the leaves
options.feedback: No live fungus is involved.

options.label: The plant is fed a glowing dye
options.feedback: The glow is produced by the plant itself.

options.label: The leaves are coated with spores
options.feedback: A coating would wash off in the first rain.

items.ok_line: The fuel was already in the plant. Only the machinery had to be added.
items.ko_line: The reason fungi were chosen over fireflies is chemical, and it is about the fuel.
items.exp_text: Fungal bioluminescence runs on caffeic acid, a molecule plants already make in quantity as part of building wood. Adding the handful of fungal genes that process it produces plants that glow steadily green without any additive — brighter than earlier attempts using firefly genes, which needed a fuel plants do not make. The glow tracks the plant's own activity, brightening around flowers and at damaged spots.

items.prompt: Why is a glowing fungus so hard to notice on an ordinary walk?

options.label: The eye needs long adjustment to the dark
options.feedback: Twenty minutes or more without any light.

options.label: It only glows a few nights a year
options.feedback: Many glow continuously for weeks.

options.label: It glows only in deep winter
options.feedback: Most are found in warm, damp months.

options.label: The light is a colour we cannot see
options.feedback: Green is the colour we see best.

items.ok_line: The fungus is glowing. Your eyes simply are not ready.
items.ko_line: The obstacle is not the fungus. It is the state of your own eyes.
items.exp_title: The problem is your eyes, not the fungus
items.exp_text: Most foxfire is far dimmer than people expect, and a fully dark-adapted eye takes twenty to thirty minutes to reach its sensitivity — a single glance at a phone screen resets the whole process. Walk into a wood with a torch and you will see nothing whatever. Sit still in the dark for half an hour and the same log can become plainly visible.
